traveler: Albertus Magnus (Albert of Lauingen, Albert the Great)
title: The Lector's Circuit: Albert of Lauingen, the Whole of Aristotle, and the Convent of the Holy Cross
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Lauingen on the Danube, the birth
stops.date_confidence: The year is not documented. German scholarship quotes Weisheipl to the effect that nothing more can be said than that Albert was born around 1200 or somewhat earlier; Italian reference works give a range between 1193 and 1206; the Linda Hall Library states flatly that his date of birth is not known. New Advent's 1205 or 1206 is one conjecture among several. Set to 1200-01-01 to open the file. The Lauingen association itself is attested only through the byname, Albertus de Lauingen.
stops.campa: A son is born to a family of the lesser Swabian nobility in Lauingen, a walled town on the north bank of the Danube in the diocese of Augsburg. No register records the day, the month, or the year. The town enters the record only because he carries its name for the rest of his life, signing and being called Albert of Lauingen. Everything else about the household is guesswork, and the sources that make his father a knight of the Bollstaedt line are late. The river runs past the walls eastward toward Regensburg, where he will one day be bishop against his will.
suggested_refs: The Albertus Magnus memorial before the town hall at Lauingen an der Donau
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'
Linda Hall Library, 'Scientist of the Day: Albertus Magnus'

stops.name: Padua, the faculty of arts
stops.date_confidence: No year is documented. The Stanford Encyclopedia says only that he likely studied at the Faculty of Arts of the University of Padua; German Wikipedia places him in Padua in 1223, the year of his entry into the order, not earlier. The 1220 anchor carried in some chronologies is supported by nothing consulted here. Set to 1222-01-01 and read as the early 1220s.
stops.campa: The young Swabian crosses the Alps to Padua, where the arts faculty teaches the logic, the natural books, and the medicine that no German cathedral school yet offers. Here the recovered Aristotle is read openly, in Latin made from the Greek and from the Arabic, together with the commentaries that came west with the translations. Padua does not make him a theologian; theology is elsewhere and comes later. It makes him a reader of Aristotle, and that is the one occupation he never afterward puts down.
suggested_refs: The medieval schools of Padua before the Basilica of Saint Anthony was begun in 1232
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Padua, the habit from Jordan of Saxony
stops.date_confidence: 1223 is secure for the entry into the order: the Stanford Encyclopedia has 'became a Dominican in 1223', German Wikipedia 'Noch 1223 trat Albertus in diesen Orden ein'. The alternative 1229 found in some chronologies is a minority reading, not a live scholarly option. That the habit came from Jordan of Saxony at Padua is traditional, carried here from a Vatican general audience of 24 March 2010, not from a contemporary record. Month and day unknown. The Marian apparition and its promise are [R], late Dominican hagiography; the Stanford Encyclopedia entry contains no mention of it and neither does New Advent, contrary to what some chronologies claim of those two sources.
stops.campa: Jordan of Saxony, second master general of the Order of Preachers and its most effective recruiter among students, comes through Padua and preaches to the scholars. Albert takes the habit from his hands. He is perhaps twenty-three, and the order he is entering is younger than he is: Dominic has been dead two years and the Preachers are barely seven years confirmed. Late Dominican hagiography adds that he afterward thought of leaving, and that the Virgin appeared to him and promised him learning if he stayed. Nothing contemporary says any such thing.
stops.quote: he received the religious habit from Bl. Jordan of Saxony
stops.quote_source: Benedict XVI, general audience of 24 March 2010, vatican.va
suggested_refs: Jordan of Saxony's letters and his Libellus on the beginnings of the Order of Preachers
sources: Benedict XVI, general audience, 24 March 2010, vatican.va
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Cologne, the novitiate at Holy Cross
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia: 'Sein Noviziat absolvierte er in Koeln.' No year is given there; 1224-01-01 is set immediately after the 1223 entry to order the segment. The coordinate is the canonical Cologne studium pin used across the atlas, 50.9407 / 6.9583. Note a discrepancy not resolved here: the German article on the Cologne Dominican convent places Heilig Kreuz at 50.9430 / 6.9543, in the Niederich quarter at the corner of Stolkgasse, some 300 metres north of the pin used.
stops.campa: He is sent north to make his novitiate at the Dominican convent of the Holy Cross in Cologne, a house planted in the Niederich quarter only a few years before, in a city of some forty thousand that is the largest in Germany and the seat of an archbishop who is also an elector of the Empire. He will leave this convent and come back to it four times across the next fifty-six years: as a student, as the founder of its school, as the arbitrator between its archbishop and its citizens, and finally as an old man dying in one of its cells.
suggested_refs: The Dominican convent of Heilig Kreuz, Cologne, suppressed in the secularization and demolished in 1804
sources: Benedict XVI, general audience, 24 March 2010, vatican.va

segments.name: The Lector's Circuit in the German Houses

stops.name: Cologne, On the Nature of the Good
stops.date_confidence: The Stanford Encyclopedia gives only 'the first half of the 1230s' and calls it 'his first published work', not the first securely datable one; the 1233 date and the 'first securely datable' description carried in some chronologies are not in the source. Set to 1232-01-01.
stops.campa: He writes On the Nature of the Good, the first work of his to circulate: a treatise on the virtues built on Aristotle's Ethics and on Cicero, arguing the good as it is actually pursued by a creature that has a body and appetites. It passes among the lectors of the province. Nothing survives to say what the desk looked like or how long the writing took, only that from here forward he does not stop, and that the finished total will run past forty folio volumes.
suggested_refs: De natura boni, in the Editio Coloniensis of the Albertus-Magnus-Institut, Bonn
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Hildesheim, the lectorship
stops.date_confidence: The Stanford Encyclopedia lists four convents for the lectorship circuit, Hildesheim, Freiburg im Breisgau, Regensburg and Strasbourg, in no fixed order and with no dates except at Freiburg. Cologne, which some chronologies add as a fifth, is where he studied rather than a lectorship in the list. 1234-01-01 orders the segment; the real sequence is not recoverable.
stops.campa: The province sends him out as lector, the friar charged with teaching theology to his own brethren in a house that has no university, no chair, and no degree to confer. At Hildesheim he lectures to perhaps a dozen men in a room off the cloister, on scripture and on the Sentences, with whatever books the convent owns. An order that exists to train preachers needs lectors more than it needs masters, and moves them from house to house without ceremony or record. The order of his four lectorships is lost. That they filled the 1230s is all anyone can say.
suggested_refs: The Dominican house at Hildesheim, one of four convents named for the lectorship circuit
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Freiburg im Breisgau, Lesemeister for two years
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia gives firm years for this one alone: 'von 1236 bis 1238 das Amt des Lesemeisters im Predigerkloster in Freiburg.' Day and month unknown, set to 01-01. The claim that his field observation belongs to these particular years is inference from the content of the later natural books, not an attested chronology.
stops.campa: At the Predigerkloster in Freiburg im Breisgau he holds the office of Lesemeister for two years, the only lectorship in the circuit that carries firm dates. Freiburg is a young town under the Zaehringen foundation, its minster tower unbuilt, its Dominican house a generation old. He teaches, and on the evidence of what he later writes he also goes out of the cloister and looks at things: fish out of the Danube, birds of the German woods, the ores of the mines, the Swabian uplands the books on plants keep returning to. Whether the looking belongs to these two years or to the twenty after them, the books do not say.
stops.quote: The aim of natural science is not simply to accept the statements of others, but to investigate the causes that are at work in nature.
stops.quote_source: Albert, De Mineralibus lib. II, tr. ii, i, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), s.v. 'Albertus Magnus'
suggested_refs: De vegetabilibus and De animalibus, whose field observations are drawn from the Rhineland and the Danube country
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Regensburg, the first lectorship
stops.date_confidence: One of the four convents the Stanford Encyclopedia names for the circuit; neither the year nor the position in sequence is given for any of them. 1238-01-01 keeps the segment in order. The coordinates are the cathedral's, and the Gothic building standing there now was begun in 1280, after his death, so the church he actually knew in this city is gone.
stops.campa: He lectures at the Dominican house of Regensburg, a Danube trading city a few days downstream from the town he was born in, in a diocese he has no reason yet to think about. He is a friar in a borrowed room with no authority beyond his learning, no salary, and no expectation of either. Twenty-two years later he will come back to this same city as its bishop, appointed over the objection of his order and of himself, and find a diocese in debt. Nothing in this first stay predicts the second.
suggested_refs: The Regensburg Dominican convent, distinct from the cathedral, whose Gothic rebuilding began only in 1280
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Strasbourg, the last of the German houses
stops.date_confidence: The fourth of the Stanford Encyclopedia's lectorship convents, undated. Set to 1239-01-01 as the last stop before the Paris transfer of the early 1240s. The coordinates are Strasbourg Cathedral, used as the nearest fixed landmark; the medieval Dominican convent site is not separately pinned in any source consulted.
stops.campa: The last of the German houses named in the circuit. Strasbourg is an imperial free city on the Ill, the cathedral choir in use and the west front not yet begun, the Dominican convent among the largest of the province. He is close to forty and has spent his whole religious life teaching small rooms of friars in provincial towns. He will come back to this city in old age to write the Metaphysica. Between the two stays lie Paris, a chair, a pupil, and a bishopric.
suggested_refs: The Dominican convent of Strasbourg, site of both his 1230s lectorship and his residence of the later 1260s
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

segments.name: Paris: the Chair and the Pupil

stops.name: Paris, Saint-Jacques: sent for the theology course
stops.date_confidence: The Stanford Encyclopedia gives only 'in the early 1240s, he was sent to the University of Paris'. No year of arrival is documented anywhere consulted; the 1241 carried in some chronologies is false precision and is used here only to order the segment. The coordinate is the canonical Couvent Saint-Jacques pin inherited byte-identical from thomas_aquinas.journey.json, 48.8472 / 2.3433, on the rue Saint-Jacques between the present rues Soufflot and Cujas.
stops.campa: The order sends him to Paris, to its convent of Saint-Jacques on the road of that name, and to the only theology faculty in Latin Christendom whose degree is honoured everywhere. He is past forty, older than the bachelors beside him, a German among Frenchmen and Italians. Saint-Jacques holds two of the faculty's chairs and a library a provincial house could never own: the Metaphysics, the Ethics complete at last, Avicenna, Averroes, Maimonides. He reads all of it.
suggested_refs: The Couvent des Jacobins on the rue Saint-Jacques, demolished between 1800 and 1849; commemorative plaque at 14 rue Soufflot
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Paris, Saint-Jacques: the mastership in theology
stops.date_confidence: 1245 is given by both the Stanford Encyclopedia and New Advent. Month and day unknown, set to 01-01. There is a source disagreement left open here: New Advent has him 'ordered to repair to Paris' in 1245 for the mastership, while the Stanford Encyclopedia has him sent to Paris in the early 1240s. The two concern arrival against promotion and are not reconciled in anything consulted.
stops.campa: He incepts as master of theology in the academic circle of Guerric of Saint-Quentin and takes the Dominican chair at Saint-Jacques, commonly called the first German of the order to reach the Paris mastership. Inception is a public act performed in front of the faculty: a disputation, a vespers, the cap, the ring, the opened book, and the oath. The German province now has a man seated in the room where the doctrine of the Latin church is fought out sentence by sentence.
stops.quote: holding the seat of the Chair of Theology at the College of St. James
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, 'Albertus Magnus', on his Paris mastership
suggested_refs: The Dominican chair for non-French masters at the Couvent Saint-Jacques, Paris
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Paris, Saint-Jacques: Thomas Aquinas under his hand
stops.date_confidence: The teacher-pupil relation from 1245 is attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia, and thomas_aquinas.journey.json independently places Thomas's arrival at Saint-Jacques in the same year. The 'dumb ox' saying is [R]: it traces to William of Tocco's Ystoria sancti Thomae de Aquino of the early fourteenth century, some fifty years after the fact, and Tocco's own Latin could not be reached in this pass, only a modern English rendering. Month set to the academic autumn.
stops.campa: A silent, heavy Italian of about twenty arrives at Saint-Jacques and is put under the master's hand. Thomas Aquinas will stay with Albert nine years, in Paris and then in Cologne, taking down his lectures on the Ethics and on the Dionysian corpus. The classmates are said to have called Thomas the dumb ox for his bulk and his silence, and the master to have answered them from the chair. The answer is not contemporary. It belongs to William of Tocco's life of Thomas, written half a century after both men were in this room.
stops.quote: You call him the dumb ox, but in his teaching he will one day produce such a bellowing that it will be heard throughout the world.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Albert of the young Thomas Aquinas; traceable to William of Tocco, Ystoria sancti Thomae de Aquino, early fourteenth century, here from a modern secondary rendering
suggested_refs: William of Tocco, Ystoria sancti Thomae de Aquino, the earliest carrier of the 'dumb ox' saying
thomas_aquinas.journey.json, stop 'Paris, the Couvent Saint-Jacques: first arrival'
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'
English Wikipedia, 'Thomas Aquinas', citing Eleonore Stump (2003)

stops.name: Paris, Saint-Jacques: the commentators
stops.date_confidence: Albert's use of Avicenna, Averroes and Maimonides is attested across his works and in the Stanford Encyclopedia's account of him; that the reading was consolidated specifically in the Paris years is inference, and 1247-01-01 orders the segment only. No atlas file exists for Averroes or Avicenna. maimonides.journey.json was checked directly and carries no reciprocal reference, so the relation runs one way: Albert reading Maimonides. The quoted Metaphysica passage was written later, at Cologne or after.
stops.campa: In the Paris years he assembles the working library of a lifetime: Aristotle in every translation obtainable, the Greek commentators, the Liber de causis, and above all the Arabic and Jewish philosophers who had the books before the Latins did. From Avicenna he takes the structure of the soul. Averroes he reads in order to refute him, and the doctrine of one intellect shared by all men will occupy him for the next thirty years. Maimonides shows him a believer reading a pagan philosopher without flinching, and he adopts that method whole.
stops.quote: Scias quod non perficitur homo in philosophia, nisi scientia duarum philosophiarum, Aristotelis et Platonis.
stops.quote_source: Albert, Metaphysica lib. I, tr. v, c. xv, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), s.v. 'Albertus Magnus'; rendered there as: a man is not perfected in philosophy except by the knowledge of both philosophies, that of Aristotle and that of Plato
suggested_refs: The Liber de causis, which Albert took for Aristotle's and which his own century would reassign
maimonides.journey.json, which carries no reciprocal reference to Albert
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Paris, the chair given up
stops.date_confidence: The regency to 1248 is attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia. That the founding of the German studium was decided at the general chapter meeting that year is standard in the literature but was not verified against a chapter act in this pass. Month set to the summer chapter season; the day is unknown.
stops.campa: He holds the regency three years, lecturing on the Sentences, disputing in the schools, beginning the Summa de creaturis. Then the order decides to plant four new general houses of study, one of them in Germany, and names him to build it. He gives up the chair he took in 1245, the only university chair he will ever hold, three years after waiting most of his life to reach it. He is about forty-eight and going back to the province he came from, to teach friars in a convent again. Thomas Aquinas is sent north with him.
suggested_refs: The Summa de creaturis, begun in the Paris regency
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Cologne, founding the studium generale
stops.date_confidence: 1248 is attested by both the Stanford Encyclopedia and New Advent. Month set to the academic autumn, day unknown. The coordinate is the canonical Cologne studium pin, 50.9407 / 6.9583, inherited byte-identical from thomas_aquinas.journey.json and used identically in nicholas_of_cusa.journey.json and heinrich_cornelius_agrippa.journey.json.
stops.campa: He comes back to Cologne to build the order's first general house of studies in German lands, at the convent where he made his novitiate twenty-four years before. Students arrive from across the province to hear a Paris master lecture on their own side of the Rhine. This is not the University of Cologne, which will be founded in 1388, more than a century after his death. It is a friars' school, answerable to the order and to no chancellor, and for a generation there is nothing else like it in Germany.
suggested_refs: The Dominican studium generale of Cologne, ancestor but not predecessor of the University of Cologne (1388)
thomas_aquinas.journey.json, stop 'Cologne, the new studium generale'
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Cologne, the lectures taken down in another man's hand
stops.date_confidence: The Cologne teaching of 1248 to 1254 and Thomas's reportationes of the Ethics and Dionysius lectures are attested and are also recorded in thomas_aquinas.journey.json. Thomas's ordination at Cologne under Konrad von Hochstaden is dated only 'probably 1250' by the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, as flagged in that same file; carried here with the same hedge. 1250-01-01 orders the segment.
stops.campa: For four years he lectures at Cologne on the Nicomachean Ethics and on the whole Dionysian corpus, and Thomas Aquinas, his assistant and master of students, writes the lectures down. What survives of those courses survives partly in the pupil's hand. In these same years the archbishop Konrad von Hochstaden ordains Thomas priest in this city. Eight years from now Albert will sit in judgment on that archbishop, at the request of the citizens he is quarrelling with.
suggested_refs: Thomas Aquinas's reportationes of Albert's Cologne lectures on the Ethics and on Dionysius
thomas_aquinas.journey.json, stop 'Cologne, ordained priest'
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Cologne, the Physica and the whole of Aristotle
stops.date_confidence: The Physica is dated c. 1251-1252 in the modern critical literature as summarized by the Stanford Encyclopedia; set to 1251-01-01, month and day unknown. The twenty-year span given for the completion of the paraphrase project is the standard estimate rather than a documented figure. The quotation is the Stanford Encyclopedia's own translation of Physica I, tr. 1, cap. 1; a variant ending circulates in some chronologies and is a paraphrase, corrected here.
stops.campa: He opens the Physica by saying plainly who asked for it and why. What he then undertakes is the whole of Aristotle rewritten, paraphrase after paraphrase, the gaps filled from his own observation and from the Arabs, until the Latin world has logic, physics, the heavens, generation and corruption, meteorology, minerals, plants, animals, the soul, and metaphysics in books a Dominican student can actually get through. He is fifty-one when he starts. It takes him twenty years.
stops.quote: Our intention, in natural science, is to satisfy as much as we can the brothers of our order who have been asking us, for now many years, to compose for them a book on physics like this one, in which they might acquire a complete knowledge of natural science and on the basis of which they might be able to understand properly the books of Aristotle.
stops.quote_source: Albert, Physica I, tr. 1, cap. 1, p. 1, l. 9-49, translated in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'
suggested_refs: The Aristotelian paraphrases, from the Physica of c. 1251 to the Metaphysica of the later 1260s
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

segments.name: The Order's Business: Worms, Anagni, Valenciennes

stops.name: Worms, elected provincial of Teutonia
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia gives the place: 'Im Jahre 1254 wurde Albert in Worms zum Provinzial der deutschsprachigen Dominikaner-Ordensprovinz Teutonia gewaehlt.' New Advent and the Stanford Encyclopedia give the year without the place, and some chronologies wrongly locate the election at Cologne; corrected here. Month and day unknown. The refusal of horses is [R], from the same late tradition that supplies the nickname Bundschuh.
stops.campa: The provincial chapter meets at Worms and elects him prior provincial of Teutonia, the German province, which reaches from the Low Countries to the Baltic and down to the Alps. The office means visitation: every house entered, every lector examined, every quarrel judged, and the whole province crossed on the order's business. Tradition says he did it on foot and refused the horses his rank allowed him. He is about fifty-four and has just been pulled off the Aristotle for the first time.
suggested_refs: The Dominican province of Teutonia, from the Low Countries to the Baltic, visited on foot
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Anagni, answering William of Saint-Amour
stops.date_confidence: New Advent: 'He journeyed to Rome in 1256'; the Master of the Sacred Palace office in that year is also given in Italian reference works. The claim that Bonaventure and the Dominican master general Humbert of Romans stood with him is carried in some chronologies but is supported by nothing consulted here: the Wikipedia articles on Anagni and on William of Saint-Amour name only Albert and Aquinas as respondents. The named companions are therefore dropped rather than hedged. Month unknown, set before the October condemnation.
stops.campa: The secular masters of Paris, led by William of Saint-Amour, have argued that the mendicant orders are illegitimate: that friars who beg instead of working are the perilous men of the last days that scripture foretold, and that they have no business holding chairs in a university. Albert travels to the papal curia at Anagni to answer it. What is at stake is whether his order may teach at all. In the same year he holds the office of Master of the Sacred Palace, house theologian to the pope.
suggested_refs: William of Saint-Amour, De periculis novissimorum temporum (1256)

stops.name: Anagni, the condemnation of the fifth of October
stops.date_confidence: Attested with a full date. New Advent: 'his book...was condemned by Pope Alexander IV on 5 October, 1256.' The English Wikipedia article on Anagni corroborates: 'Alexander officially condemned the work in Anagni on October 5, 1256.'
stops.campa: Alexander IV condemns De periculis novissimorum temporum at Anagni and orders the book burned. William loses his chair and is put out of France. The friars keep the schools, and the order Albert entered thirty-three years earlier is confirmed in the universities. The argument itself does not die with the book: the secular masters will come at the mendicants again within twenty years, and the same charge will be laid in the same faculty by men not yet born.
stops.quote: Alexander officially condemned the work in Anagni on October 5, 1256
suggested_refs: The bull of 5 October 1256 condemning De periculis novissimorum temporum

stops.name: Cologne, the provincialate laid down
stops.date_confidence: New Advent: 'He resigned the office of Provincial in 1257.' The month is not documented; June is set as the customary chapter season. The natural-history examples named here come from the content of De animalibus and De vegetabilibus and are not tied by any source to a dated moment of composition.
stops.campa: Three years of visitation are enough and he lays the office down, coming back to Cologne to teach and to write, which is the one thing he asks for and the thing he is least often allowed to keep. The paraphrases resume where the office interrupted them: the books on animals, on plants, on minerals, full of things he has looked at himself. He measures things and he cuts them open. He reports what a fisherman told him, and then says whether he believes it.
stops.quote_source: Albert, De Vegetabilibus VI, tr. ii, i, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), s.v. 'Albertus Magnus', glossed there as: experiment is the only safe guide in such investigations
suggested_refs: De animalibus, De vegetabilibus and De mineralibus, the observational core of the paraphrase project
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Cologne, the Great Arbitration
stops.date_confidence: The 1258 arbitration between Konrad von Hochstaden and the citizens of Cologne is documented and is carried in the Wikipedia article as 'der Grosse Schied'; the specialist study cited in the dossier, Groten 2011, was not fetched in this pass. Month and day are not established. The coordinate is Cologne Cathedral, used as the fixed landmark for the archiepiscopal court, and deliberately differs from the studium pin used on the convent stops in this file.
stops.campa: Cologne's citizens and their archbishop, Konrad von Hochstaden, have been in open conflict over jurisdiction, tolls, and the right to judge. Both sides accept the friar as arbitrator. He holds no office in the city and has nothing behind the award but the agreement of the parties to be bound by it. What he hands down, remembered as the Grosser Schied, does not abolish the quarrel. It specifies it: which court hears what, who holds which right, where the archbishop's power stops and the burghers' begins.
suggested_refs: The Grosser Schied of 1258 between Archbishop Konrad von Hochstaden and the citizens of Cologne

stops.name: Valenciennes, the plan of studies
stops.date_confidence: The 1259 general chapter at Valenciennes and the five-man commission are given by the English Wikipedia article on Albert, and the Valenciennes article independently confirms the chapter and Aquinas's participation. Month and day unknown; the specific building within the town is not named in anything consulted.
stops.campa: At the general chapter of Valenciennes he sits with Thomas Aquinas, Bonushomo Britto, Florentius, and Peter of Tarentaise, who will one day be pope, to draw up the whole plan of studies for the order. What the five produce gives philosophy a formal place in the training of preachers: the arts are not a distraction from theology but the road into it, and no friar is to be sent to theology without them. Every Dominican house in Europe will teach on this scheme.
suggested_refs: The ratio studiorum of the general chapter of Valenciennes, 1259

stops.name: Regensburg, made bishop against his will
stops.date_confidence: New Advent: 'In the year 1260 he was appointed Bishop of Ratisbon'; the Stanford Encyclopedia corroborates the year. The precise day, 5 January, is carried from the dossier and was not independently confirmed in this pass. That the appointment ran against the preference of the Dominican leadership and against his own inclination is reported by New Advent; no named individual's plea is attested in anything consulted, so none is given here.
stops.campa: Alexander IV names him bishop of Regensburg, over the objection of the Dominican leadership and against his own inclination. He is about sixty and has never held a see or wanted one. The diocese is in debt, its clergy unreformed, its administration in disorder, and its business is exactly the sort of business he has spent forty years arranging to be left out of. He accepts because a friar under obedience accepts, and goes down the Danube to a city he last entered as an unknown lector teaching a dozen brothers in a room off a cloister.
suggested_refs: The see of Regensburg in 1260, indebted and under reform pressure
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: The Regensburg diocese, the hobnailed shoe
stops.date_confidence: [R] for the nickname. The dossier characterizes 'Bundschuh' as later hagiographic tradition and it could not be confirmed against any independently fetched source in this pass, including the English Wikipedia article that the dossier itself cites. The administrative reform of the diocese is generally reported but is not itemized in any source consulted. Date set to 1260-06-01 to sit inside the episcopate.
stops.campa: He puts the diocese back in order in under two years: the debts audited, the estates recovered, the clergy visited house by house. Later biographers give him a name for the way he went about it, Bundschuh, the hobnailed shoe, because he is supposed to have crossed his diocese on foot in a friar's habit rather than riding out with an episcopal train. A Dominican might well have walked. The nickname is another matter. No contemporary document uses it.
suggested_refs: The Bundschuh nickname, attested only in later hagiographic biographies
sources: dossier characterization, tagged [R] and not independently verified

stops.name: Orvieto, released by Urban IV
stops.date_confidence: Four sources give 1262 for the release: the Stanford Encyclopedia ('was granted his request to be relieved of his position in 1262'), New Advent, Italian Wikipedia, and German Wikipedia, which supplies the month: 'Dort entpflichtete ihn der Papst im Februar 1262 von seinem Amt als Bischof von Regensburg.' Chronologies giving 1261 and placing the curia at Viterbo are wrong twice over: German Wikipedia places Albert at Urban IV's court in Orvieto, and Urban IV was not elected until 29 August 1261, so no journey to seek release from him can predate that. The Viterbo Palazzo dei Papi was in any case only completed around 1266. Day unknown.
stops.campa: He travels to the curia of Urban IV at Orvieto and asks to be let go. In February the pope releases him from Regensburg. He has held the see about two years, and will spend the remaining eighteen years of his life as a friar again, with no diocese and no chair, doing whatever the pope and the order set in front of him. He keeps the title of bishop and the right to consecrate churches and altars, and he is still consecrating them in the Rhineland eighteen years later.
suggested_refs: The papal court of Urban IV at Orvieto, which the pope divided with Viterbo
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

segments.name: Preaching, Teaching, and the Long Return to Cologne

stops.name: The German-speaking lands, preaching the crusade
stops.date_confidence: The commission is attested for 1263: 'Pope Urban IV requested he preach the Eighth Crusade in German-speaking countries' (English Wikipedia). The coordinates 50.0 / 9.0 are a rough centroid of the German-speaking Empire and mark no specific place; no preaching station is named in any source consulted, which is a real gap. The February start is carried from the dossier and was not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: Urban IV commissions him to preach the crusade for the Holy Land throughout the German-speaking lands. Preaching the cross is not scholarly work. It is recruitment, fundraising, and the taking of vows in market squares, and the pope wants a famous German doing it in German. For some twenty months a bishop without a see, sixty-three years old, travels the Empire. Not one town where he preached is named in anything that survives. The commission ends when the pope who issued it dies in October 1264.
stops.quote: preach the Eighth Crusade in German-speaking countries
suggested_refs: The crusade preaching commission of Urban IV in Germany, 1263-1264
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Wuerzburg, the Metaphysica begun
stops.date_confidence: The Stanford Encyclopedia gives the pair together: 'taught in Wuerzburg and Strasbourg (1264-1269)'. How those five years divided between the two cities is not documented anywhere consulted. Set to 1265-01-01. Coordinates are the Wuerzburg city center; no specific convent building was identified in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: With the commission lapsed he settles at Wuerzburg on the Main and teaches in the Dominican house there. The Metaphysica, last and largest of the Aristotelian paraphrases, belongs to this stretch of years: a running commentary on the book that asks what being is, written by a man in his middle sixties with no chair, no diocese, and no fixed house. He is by now the most cited living authority in the Latin schools, and he is working out of a provincial convent on a river.
stops.quote: Whoever believes that Aristotle was a god, must also believe that he never erred. But if one believe that Aristotle was a man, then doubtless he was liable to error just as we are.
stops.quote_source: Albert, Physica lib. VIII, tr. 1, xiv, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), s.v. 'Albertus Magnus'
suggested_refs: The Metaphysica, written across the Wuerzburg and Strasbourg years of 1264-1269
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Strasbourg, thirty years on
stops.date_confidence: Part of the Stanford Encyclopedia's 'Wuerzburg and Strasbourg (1264-1269)'; the year within that span is not fixed and 1267-01-01 orders the segment. Coordinates repeat the Strasbourg Cathedral landmark used for the 1230s lectorship stop in this file. The characterization of him as a general consultant to the province is not a documented series of cases.
stops.campa: He is back in Strasbourg, some thirty years after lecturing here as an unknown lector, in a city whose cathedral has grown a nave since he left it and whose west front is still only a plan on paper. He writes, and he is consulted. What the province sends him now are the questions nobody else in it can settle, the way Cologne sent him its quarrel with its archbishop. No document names one of those cases. That he served as a general consultant to the province is a characterization drawn from his standing, not a docket anyone has produced.
suggested_refs: The Dominican convent of Strasbourg, his residence twice, three decades apart
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Cologne, the last return
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia: 'Um 1269 kehrte er endgueltig zurueck in das Dominikanerkloster', with 'um', around. Some chronologies add that the master general John of Vercelli recalled him as 'lector emeritus'; neither the man nor the title appears in the Stanford Encyclopedia, New Advent, or German Wikipedia, so both are dropped here rather than hedged. Month unknown.
stops.campa: Around 1269 he returns for good to the Dominican convent at Cologne, where he made his novitiate as a young man and founded the studium as a Paris master. He is about sixty-nine. For eleven years he writes, preaches, consecrates altars and churches across the Rhineland, and arbitrates for whoever brings him a quarrel. He holds no office again, and asks for none. The German sources put the return at around 1269 and cannot fix the month. He stays in the house until he dies in it.
stops.quote: In studying nature we have not to inquire how God the Creator may, as He freely wills, use His creatures to work miracles and thereby show forth His power: we have rather to inquire what Nature with its immanent causes can naturally bring to pass.
stops.quote_source: Albert, De Coelo et Mundo I, tr. iv, x, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), s.v. 'Albertus Magnus'
suggested_refs: The Cologne convent of Holy Cross in his final decade, 1269-1280
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Cologne, the memoir sent to Paris
stops.date_confidence: New Advent: 'In the year 1270 he sent a memoir to Paris.' The identification of that memoir with the controversy over the unity of the intellect follows the Stanford Encyclopedia's account of his continued engagement with the intellect disputes; the two are not explicitly joined in anything consulted, so the connection is inference. Month unknown.
stops.campa: From Cologne he sends a treatise down to Paris, into the fight over whether there is one intellect for all men or one for each. Averroes had argued the first and the Paris arts masters had taken it up; Albert has been refuting it since before his own pupil held a chair. He states the stake without ornament: if the intellect is one and shared, then no particular soul survives its own body. He is seventy. The argument he is answering is one he first took up in his forties, in Paris, in the room the treatise is addressed to.
suggested_refs: De unitate intellectus contra Averroistas, Albert's anti-Averroist intervention
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Cologne, word from Fossanova
stops.date_confidence: Aquinas's death on 7 March 1274 at Fossanova is secure and is carried in thomas_aquinas.journey.json. The weeping is [R], a later devotional narrative with no contemporary witness, so flagged in the English Wikipedia article and in the dossier. The stop sits at Albert's Cologne pin and not at Fossanova, because Albert was not there.
stops.campa: Word reaches Cologne that Thomas Aquinas is dead at Fossanova, at forty-nine, on the road south to the council at Lyons that Albert will attend without him. Albert is seventy-four and has outlived by twenty-five years the pupil he taught for nine. The tradition says he wept whenever the name was spoken afterward, and that he defended the writings while the man was still too recently dead to defend himself. The weeping has no contemporary witness. The outliving is a fact.
suggested_refs: thomas_aquinas.journey.json, for the death at Fossanova, 7 March 1274
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Lyon, the Second Council
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia records a specific act: 'trat er 1274 auf dem Zweiten Konzil von Lyon fuer die Anerkennung Rudolfs von Habsburg als deutscher Koenig ein.' New Advent lists the Council of Lyons (1274) among his activities. Some chronologies hedge his participation as less documented than devotional accounts claim; that hedge is not sustainable against the German source and is dropped. The council opened 7 May 1274, and that date is used; his own arrival is not separately dated.
stops.campa: At the Second Council of Lyons the old bishop of Regensburg speaks for the recognition of Rudolf of Habsburg as king of the Germans. The Empire has been without an undisputed king for twenty years, and the council is also negotiating the reunion with the Greeks that Thomas Aquinas was travelling toward when he died two months before it opened. Albert was born under Hohenstaufen rule and has served four popes. He comes down out of Germany at seventy-four to argue for the man who ends the interregnum.
suggested_refs: The Second Council of Lyons, opened 7 May 1274, and the recognition of Rudolf of Habsburg
sources: Benedict XVI, general audience, 24 March 2010, vatican.va

stops.name: Paris, the condemnation and the journey nobody can confirm
stops.date_confidence: The evidence splits and is left split. New Advent asserts the journey as fact, '1277: Journeyed to Paris to defend St. Thomas's writings', as does Italian Wikipedia. The Stanford Encyclopedia entry on Albert does not mention any such journey, in either of two fetches made for this file, and modern biographers treat it as unconfirmed. Tagged [R] for the journey itself; the condemnation of 7 March 1277 is [A]. Coordinate is the canonical Saint-Jacques pin, used on the assumption of the journey, not as evidence for it.
stops.campa: On the seventh of March, Etienne Tempier, bishop of Paris, condemns two hundred and nineteen propositions, and some of them touch what Thomas Aquinas taught. The older Catholic reference works say that Albert, seventy-seven years old, made the journey to Paris himself to defend his dead pupil's writings in the faculty where he had once held the chair. The Stanford Encyclopedia says nothing about any such journey. Nothing in the record decides it. The condemnation is not in doubt; the old man on the road is.
suggested_refs: The condemnation of 219 propositions by Etienne Tempier, Paris, 7 March 1277
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great' (silent on the journey)

segments.name: The Testament, the Grave, and the Legends

stops.name: Cologne, the testament
stops.date_confidence: Sources conflict on the year and the conflict is flagged rather than resolved. New Advent puts the will in 1278, 'in which year he drew up his testament'; German Wikipedia refers to 'seinem Testament aus dem Jahr 1279'. January 1279 is adopted here, with 1278 recorded as the competing reading. The detail about the choir exceeding mendicant building norms comes from the dossier and was not checked against a transcription of the will.
stops.campa: He draws up his will, declaring himself sound in mind and in body, and leaves money to the Dominican church of Cologne. The bequest helps pay for a choir large enough to strain the order's own rules against grand building, in a church belonging to friars who are not supposed to look rich. He is about seventy-nine. Within two years he will not be able to hold a sentence in his head, and the clause about being sound in mind will stand as the last legal statement he ever makes about himself. He signs as brother Albert, once bishop of Regensburg.
suggested_refs: The testament of 1278 or 1279 and the choir of the Cologne Dominican church it helped fund

stops.name: Cologne, the memory goes
stops.date_confidence: The decline is reported (English Wikipedia, '1278 - Health declined'; New Advent, 'Some time after 1278... he suffered a lapse of memory') and presented in both as ordinary aging, not as a fulfilled prophecy. The Marian apparition and the promise of forgetfulness are [R]: genuine Dominican hagiography, but absent from the Stanford Encyclopedia and from New Advent, contrary to what some chronologies claim of those sources. The Kierkegaard line is quoted here from the English Wikipedia article; Kierkegaard's own text was not fetched. Date set between the testament and the death.
stops.campa: In his last two years the memory goes and he stops writing. New Advent presents it as the ordinary decline of a man near eighty. Dominican hagiography presents it as the second half of a bargain: the Virgin, appearing to the young friar who wanted to leave the order, promising him learning on the condition that it be taken back before the end, so that he should not die a philosopher. No early source carries that story. What is recorded is that a man who had written forty volumes stopped.
stops.quote: [Albertus] arrogantly boasted of his speculation before the deity and suddenly became stupid.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Soren Kierkegaard, The Concept of Anxiety, as quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Albertus Magnus'; Kierkegaard's own text was not consulted
suggested_refs: The late Dominican hagiography of the Marian apparition and the promised loss of memory
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great' (silent on the apparition)

stops.name: Cologne, death in the cell
stops.date_confidence: Attested: New Advent, 'died at Cologne, 15 November 1280', corroborated by the Stanford Encyclopedia and by Wikipedia. That he died sitting in his cell at the convent of the Holy Cross follows the Vatican general audience of 24 March 2010; that dedication is more specific than the plain 'Dominican convent' used in the other sources, and the discrepancy in naming is noted rather than resolved. No cause of death is named anywhere consulted.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of November, in the year 1280, he dies in his cell at the convent of the Holy Cross, among the brethren, about eighty years old. No account names a disease. He has been a Dominican fifty-seven years, the last two of them without the memory to write. The dedication of the house to the Holy Cross comes from a Vatican audience of 2010; the older reference works say only that he died at Cologne, and nothing decides between them. The brethren in the room are not named, and no source records what was said in it.
stops.quote: He died in his cell at the convent of the Holy Cross, Cologne, in 1280
stops.quote_source: Benedict XVI, general audience of 24 March 2010, vatican.va
suggested_refs: The convent of the Holy Cross, Cologne, where he made his novitiate and where he died
sources: Benedict XVI, general audience, 24 March 2010, vatican.va
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'

stops.name: Cologne, buried in the choir
stops.date_confidence: Burial in the choir of the Dominican church is attested by New Advent and corroborated in the standard modern treatments. The date of the funeral is not recorded anywhere consulted; 17 November is set two days after the death purely to order the file. The near-contemporary praise quoted here is by his own pupil Ulrich Engelbert; note that some chronologies attribute the sentence to the Stanford Encyclopedia, which does not contain it.
stops.campa: They bury him in the choir of the Dominican church, the place a bishop and a master is owed, in a building his own legacy is helping to raise and which is not yet finished over him. His pupil Ulrich Engelbert had already set him down as the wonder of the age while he was still alive to read it. The grave becomes a Cologne fixture at once. Pilgrims come to it for three centuries before Rome allows them a beatification, and for six and a half before Rome grants a canonization.
stops.quote: Vir in omni scientia adeo divinus, ut nostri temporis stupor et miraculum congrue vocari possit.
stops.quote_source: Ulrich Engelbert (Ulrich of Strasbourg), De summo bono tr. III, iv, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), s.v. 'Albertus Magnus'; a man so godlike in every science that he may fittingly be called the wonder and miracle of our age
suggested_refs: Ulrich Engelbert of Strasbourg, De summo bono, written by a pupil in Albert's own lifetime

stops.name: Cologne, the brazen head
stops.date_confidence: [R], legend, with no contemporary source and no artifact. The dossier and the English Wikipedia article on the brazen head both record the association without identifying the earliest text that fixes it on Albert rather than on the other figures of the same legend family. Dated 1281-01-01, just after the death, purely to place the stop; the legend has no date and grows through the later Middle Ages.
stops.campa: The legend says he worked thirty years on a head of brass that could speak and answer, and that Thomas Aquinas, finding it talking in the workshop, broke it with a stick because the chatter was disturbing his study. No contemporary source describes such a thing and no fragment of it exists. The same story gets told about Gerbert of Aurillac, about Robert Grosseteste, and about others: it attaches itself to whichever man a given century has decided knew too much.
suggested_refs: The brazen-head legend family, attached variously to Gerbert of Aurillac, Robert Grosseteste and others

stops.name: Cologne, the books he did not write
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the pseudo-Albertine attribution problem, which is documented; [R] for the philosopher's-stone legend. The chronological impossibility is flagged in the English Wikipedia article itself. Dated 1350-01-01 as a midpoint of the fourteenth to sixteenth century growth of the pseudonymous corpus; no single date applies.
stops.campa: A large body of alchemical and magical writing begins to circulate under his name after his death, the Secreta Alberti and the Experimenta Alberti among them, forged onto him because the name sells. With it grows the legend that he found the philosopher's stone and handed the secret to Thomas Aquinas shortly before dying. Thomas died in 1274 and Albert in 1280, so the transfer cannot have run in that direction. What he wrote himself about transmutation, in De mineralibus, denies that art can produce a substantial form at all.
stops.quote: Art alone cannot produce a substantial form.
stops.quote_source: Albert, De Mineralibus lib. II, dist. 3, quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), s.v. 'Albertus Magnus', in its account of his rejection of alchemical transmutation
suggested_refs: The pseudo-Albertine corpus: Secreta Alberti, Experimenta Alberti, and the Liber aggregationis
sources: David A. Katz, An Illustrated History of Alchemy and Early Chemistry (1978), cited in English Wikipedia

stops.name: Cologne, the tomb opened before witnesses
stops.date_confidence: [R] on the exact date. The 1483 translation is treated as documented across the cult literature, but this pass could not independently verify the day, 11 January 1483, from a fresh fetch. The story of an incorrupt body found at an opening three years after the burial is legend, flagged as such in the English Wikipedia article, which reports the 1483 finding of a skeleton against it.
stops.campa: The grave is opened before witnesses and the remains examined. There is a skeleton. Two hundred and three years have passed since the burial. A story had been circulating that at an earlier opening, three years after the burial, the body was found whole and uncorrupted, which is what the fourteenth century expected of a saint. The order writes down what is actually there and puts it back. Both accounts stay in circulation afterward, side by side. The day given for the opening, the eleventh of January, is the one the cult literature repeats and the one this pass could not confirm.
suggested_refs: The ceremonial translation of Albert's remains at Cologne, 1483

stops.name: Rome, canonized and made a Doctor of the Church
stops.date_confidence: 16 December 1931 is given by the Stanford Encyclopedia; New Advent has the year, 'he was finally canonized in 1931'. The 1622 beatification under Gregory XV is attested by New Advent. The roughly 830-page Positio and the 1927-1931 campaign are carried from the dossier and were not independently verified in this pass. Coordinates are Vatican City generally; the room of promulgation is not identified in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Pius XI makes Albert a saint and a Doctor of the Church in a single act, six hundred and fifty-one years after the death, on a dossier of some eight hundred and thirty pages assembled over four years by German Catholics and the Dominicans. Gregory XV had beatified him in 1622 and then three centuries had passed with nothing. The form used is equipollent canonization, which does not investigate whether a cult exists. It records that one has existed for six hundred years without waiting to be asked.
suggested_refs: The Positio for the canonization of Albertus Magnus, 1927-1931
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'
Benedict XVI, general audience, 24 March 2010, vatican.va

stops.name: Rome, patron of the natural sciences
stops.date_confidence: 1941 is attested by the Stanford Encyclopedia, 'made patron saint of natural scientists in 1941 by Pius XII', and by the Vatican general audience of 24 March 2010. Month and day unknown. The Albertus-Magnus-Institut's own site confirms its 1931 founding, its Bonn location under the Archdiocese of Cologne, and the Editio Coloniensis as its purpose, but gives neither the edition's start year nor its volume count; the commonly cited 1951 is therefore not asserted here. Jammy's Lyon edition of 1651 in 21 folio volumes and Borgnet's Paris edition of 1890-1899 in 38 are attested.
stops.campa: Pius XII names him patron of students and practitioners of the natural sciences. The Albertus-Magnus-Institut, founded at Bonn ten years earlier under the archdiocese of Cologne, is already at work on the harder question of what he actually wrote, against two older printed collections that are complete and unreliable: Jammy's twenty-one folio volumes at Lyon in 1651, and Borgnet's thirty-eight at Paris in the 1890s. The critical edition is still not finished.
suggested_refs: The Editio Coloniensis of the Albertus-Magnus-Institut, Bonn, still incomplete
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert the Great'
Benedict XVI, general audience, 24 March 2010, vatican.va

stops.name: Saint Andreas, Cologne: the Roman sarcophagus
stops.date_confidence: The relics at Saint Andreas and the third-century Roman sarcophagus are attested by the English Wikipedia article on the church, whose coordinates 50.9417 / 6.9539 are used exactly. The transfer date is contested and is left contested: German Wikipedia's Albert article says the bones have rested there since the suppression of the convent in 1804, while its article on the Cologne Dominican convent dates the transfer to 1802, with the church closed 28 September 1802 and demolished in 1804. Read as 1802-1804. The 1954 installation in the sarcophagus comes from the dossier alone, is not independently confirmed, and is used here only as the stop's date.
stops.campa: The Dominican convent was suppressed in the secularization and its church pulled down; the bones went a few streets across the old town to Saint Andreas, and they have not moved since. In the crypt they lie inside a Roman sarcophagus cut in the third century, a thousand years before Albert was born, for somebody whose name nobody now knows. A second relic is kept at Saint Stephen's in Nijmegen. On the square named for him at the university his own city founded a century after his death, his bronze stands with three replicas of it scattered from Jena to Houston.
stops.quote: In the crypt of the church lies a Roman sarcophagus from the 3rd century, which holds the remains of the 13th-century theologian and natural philosopher St. Albertus Magnus
suggested_refs: The crypt of St. Andreas, Cologne
Gerhard Marcks's bronze on Albertus-Magnus-Platz, University of Cologne, 50.9281 / 6.9286, with replicas at Jena, the University of the Andes, and the University of Houston
